chloride anion is essential for active intestinal transport of calcium.
the active transport of calcium in the rat duodenum is an anion-dependent, sodium-independent, saturable process.
calcium is transported against its electrochemical gradient in rat duodena and this transport is dependent on the chloride anion, but not on the presence of phosphate.

the mechanism of intestinal calcium transport and the role of anions in this process.
the mechanism of active calcium transport across the intestinal epithelium of the rat.
the role of anions in calcium transport in the small intestine.

calcium transport in rat duodena is a sodium-cation-dependent, chloride-anion-dependent, energy-dependent process that moves calcium across the epithelium against concentration and electrotensional gradients.
the active transport of calcium in duodenum is an energy-dependent cation-oriented saturable process that requires anions.
the active transport of calcium in the intestine is a sodium-dependent process which requires the participation of a specific anion.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the transport of calcium in duodenum is a process requiring sodium, chloride and energy.
in rat small intestine there are two anions which are essential for calcium transport: phosphate in distal ileum and chloride in duodenum.
in rat duodena calcium transport is dependent on sodium ion but not on chloride ion, whereas calcium transport in distal ileum requires sodium and chloride ions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
calcium transport in rat duodenuum requires anions.
calcium transport is a saturable process and that the anion requirement is not due to an electrogenic transport of calcium but to the requirement for an anion for the transport process.
calcium transport in duodenum is a complex process involving several factors, and that chloride is an essential component of the transport system.
